title: Throughput benchmarking harness and methodology
content:
Purpose / scope:
This doc captures the benchmarking harness and methodology we use to measure steady-state throughput for the serving runtime. Focus is on repeatable measurement of requests/sec and tokens/sec under representative production-style load profiles, plus guidance on warmup, priming, and artifacts to retain for post-mortem analysis.

Goals:
- Produce stable, repeatable throughput numbers for model variants (fp16, int8/4bit quantized) across hardware (A100, H100, T4).
- Surface host- vs device-side bottlenecks (kernel time, memcpy, queueing, batching overhead).
- Define run configs, warmup requirements, and artifact collection to enable audits and regression detection.
- Minimize noise and document what to pin in the environment for reproducibility.

High-level harness architecture:
- Coordinator (bench runner): orchestrates experiment runs, uploads artifacts to GCS, records env metadata (CUDA, driver, container digest, commit SHA).
- Load generator (loadgen): can drive either QPS-based or concurrency-based profiles. Support for steady, ramp, spike, and diurnal patterns.
- Inference cluster: 1+ serving replicas with pinned model version. Instrumented with Prometheus and tracing (OpenTelemetry).
- Profilers: Nsight Systems (system traces), PyTorch/TensorRT profiler for kernel-level timing, CUPTI or NVIDIA tools for GPU counters.

Reproducibility checklist (things to pin):
- Model commit hash and quantization config (quantize-config.json).
- Container image digest and package versions (torch, triton, cuda, cudnn).
- GPU driver and CUDA toolkit versions.
- Serving runtime commit SHA and exact command-line args.
- Network topology: same subnet, NIC config, and bandwidth shaping.
- Loadgen binary version and seed for sampling prompts.

Warmup and priming strategy:
- Why warmup matters: first N requests warmup JITs/kernels, populate KV cache, and allow auto-batching to reach steady patterns. If you don't warm up you will under-report throughput.
- Warmup policy (recommended default):
  - Step 1: KV priming: issue a deterministic set of 200 short requests per model variant to populate caches. These can be single-turn prompts with average sequence length.
  - Step 2: Kernel warmup: ramp QPS from 10% to target QPS over 3 minutes (or 1000 requests), whichever is longer.
  - Step 3: Steady-state hold: after ramp, run a stabilization window of 2x the expected measurement window and discard these samples from metrics.
- Warmup heuristics by model size: larger models (>= 70B) often need longer priming (e.g., 500 requests) because tokenization, KV state setup and kernel autotuning produce additional costs.

Load profiles and configs:
- Config parameters to capture in every run (sample loadgen YAML):
  - model: <model-name>@<commit>
  - target_mode: qps | concurrency
  - target_value: 200  # qps or concurrency
  - seq_len_distribution: path/to/seq-dist.json  # histogram of seq lengths
  - prompt_corpus: path/to/prompts.jsonl
  - payload_tokens_mean: 64
  - batch_size: auto | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8
  - max_latency_ms: 3000
  - warmup: {"kv_priming": 200, "ramp_minutes": 3, "stabilize_minutes": 6}
  - repeats: 5
  - inter_run_cooldown_seconds: 120

- Typical load profiles we exercise:
  - Steady-state QPS: constant QPS (useful for measuring tokens/sec at a target load).
  - Concurrency-driven: N concurrent clients issuing requests as fast as possible (reveals queuing/backpressure).
  - Ramp: linear qps ramp from 0 -> target over configurable time (observes autoscaler or batching warmup effects).
  - Spike: short high-QPS bursts to test graceful degradation and fallback policies.

Repeatability and statistical significance:
- Always run each configuration at least 5 times (repeats) and report mean, std, and median. If std/mean > 5% investigate noise sources.
- Use the middle 60-80% of the duration (after ramp and stabilize windows) as the measurement window to avoid startup/teardown artifacts.
- Save raw per-request logs (timestamp, latency_ms, token_count, request_id, model_version) for each run and keep them alongside aggregated CSVs.

Metrics to collect (minimum):
- Request-level: requests/sec, tokens/sec, p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9 latency (ms), tail latency distribution.
- GPU/device: utilization (%), memory usage (MB), SM occupancy, achieved occupancy counters, active kernels timeline.
- Host: CPU % (per-core), kernel time vs user time, memcpy bytes/sec, network tx/rx (MB/s), disk IO if using local cache.
- Runtime internals: batching stats (avg batch size, batch distribution), queue lengths, queue wait time, KV cache hit rate.
- System traces: nsight system timeline to map host events to GPU kernels.

How we interpret results (quick heuristics):
- Low GPU utilization + high tokens/sec variance -> host or memcpy bottleneck.
- High GPU utilization + low achieved tokens/sec -> kernel-level inefficiency (investigate kernel launch / config / quantization).
- Large tail latency with low median -> queuing or priority inversion; check batching behavior and mutex contention in runtime.
- Throughput drops when enabling quantization -> check packing/unpacking overhead and whether integer kernels are optimized for the target hardware.

Artifacts to store per-run (required):
- env.txt (cuda, driver, container digest, git SHAs)
- loadgen-config.yaml (exact parameters used)
- raw-requests.log (newline JSON per request)
- aggregated-metrics.csv (per-run aggregated stats)
- profiler-trace.nsight.zip or .qdrep
- runtime-metrics-prom.json (Prometheus scrape for the run window)
- perf-notes.md (analyst notes, anomalies observed)

Recommended tooling and commands:
- Loadgen: python tools/loadgen.py --config loadgen-config.yaml --outdir /tmp/bench-123
- Start profiler: Nsight Systems (collector) – capture around measurement window only to limit overhead.
- GPU counters: ncu or nvprof replacement flows for low-overhead sampling.
- Prometheus/grafana: ensure high-resolution scrape (5s or less) for benchmark runs.

Common gotchas / caveats:
- Auto-batching can make QPS->latency relationship non-linear. Measure both qps and effective batch-size histogram.
- Sequence length distribution matters a lot. Small changes in token-length mix can change throughput by 10-40%.
- Cache priming: if you benchmark without priming, you'll get a lower bound that doesn't reflect steady-state production behavior.
- System noise: cloud neighbors, background GC, or host processes can introduce outliers. Use dedicated hosts for benchmark runs when possible.

Analysis checklist (post-run):
1) Confirm env pins match recorded env.txt.
2) Plot time-series: qps, latency p95/p99, GPU util. Look for drift or correlated drops.
3) Inspect batch size distribution and queue wait times.
4) Correlate profiler kernel timelines with latency spikes.
5) If regression observed, run A/B with a narrow diff (single commit or single config change) and collect traces for both.

Runbook (quick steps to run a new experiment):
1) Create a new bench ticket (JIRA INF-xxx) documenting model, hardware, and hypothesis.
2) Prepare loadgen-config.yaml and attach sample prompts + seq-dist.
3) Ensure cluster is clean (no unrelated services). Pin container digest.
4) Run warmup: kv priming + ramp.
5) Execute N repeats (default 5) with cooldown between runs.
6) Collect artifacts and upload to GCS under gs://redwood-performance/INF-xxx/; update the ticket with links.
7) Run analysis notebook (notebook path in linked artifacts) to generate plots and produce perf-notes.md.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Evaluate lower-overhead GPU counters for continuous benchmarking (currently Nsight capture adds non-trivial overhead for long runs). (JIRA: INF-240)
- Add support for token-level streaming latency measurement (we currently measure only request-level).
- Automate comparison report generation (A vs B) and add to PR checks for runtime changes.

Appendix: Example minimal loadgen-config.yaml snippet:

model: redwood/phi-2@sha256:abcd1234
target_mode: qps
target_value: 300
seq_len_distribution: seq-dist-prod-64.json
prompt_corpus: prompts/news-1k.jsonl
batch_size: auto
warmup:
  kv_priming: 200
  ramp_minutes: 3
  stabilize_minutes: 6
repeats: 5

Notes: commit this config alongside the artifacts for traceability.

If you run into weird results ping #perf on Slack and assign INF-124 to triage.

-- Ethan (eng-serving-runtime)
